The Los Angeles Dodgers clinched the NL West for the 14th time in their last 15 seasons with an 8-2 win over the Cincinnati Reds on Thursday. Justin Wrobleski pitched three perfect innings, Freddie Freeman continued to heat up, Miguel Rojas hit just his fourth homer of the year, but the Dodgers' top performer, not just in the series finale, but over the Dodgers' last 10 games was Kyle Tucker.
He homered in his first at-bat on Thursday to give the Dodgers an early 2-0 lead. By the end of the game, he'd gone 4-for-5 with the homer, two doubles, three RBI, and ended up a triple shy of the cycle.
After a long season of struggles and fans and writers alike wondering aloud if the Dodgers made a huge mistake signing him to his absurd four-year, $240 million contract, Tucker seems to have turned back into his old self at just the right time.
The Dodgers, while still heavy favorites to win the World Series, have a whole host of weaknesses their upcoming postseason opponents can (and will) identify and exploit. But Tucker earning back his old King Tuck moniker in LA would add an extra bite the lineup expected but hasn't seen most of this season.
However, there's a caveat to all of this that Dodgers fans shouldn't ignore. LA has played seven of their last 10 games against the Reds, one of the worst teams in the National League.
Kyle Tucker's newfound success for the Dodgers has to be tempered by one unavoidable fact
Before coming into this nine-game stretch, Tucker hit .143 with a .628 OPS against the Detroit Tigers, St. Louis Cardinals, and Washington Nationals. All are inferior opponents to the Dodgers and some even had worse records than the Reds by the time they saw the Dodgers. But none had the NL or AL's second-worst run differential like Cincinnati.
Going into this series, Cincinnati had a staggering -148 run differential. Their pitching staff's collective ERA is 4.87 and WHIP is 1.45, the third-worst in baseball in both categories. Of the four starters the Dodgers faced during this series, only Andrew Abbott had an ERA under 5.00 (4.78).
The Dodgers' last nine games should be a greater test of Tucker's mettle, and will prove whether or not this hot streak was purely incidental. Six inter-division games against the San Francisco Giants and three against the San Diego Padres are surely going to give the Dodgers more grief, as games against those teams often do, and may expose this recent surge as being nothing more than a flash in the pan.

Los Dodgers vuelven a reinar en el Oeste de la Nacional y buscan un tricampeonato pese a lesiones
CINCINNATI — Los Dodgers de Los Ángeles aseguraron su quinto título consecutivo de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional y el 13ro en las últimas 14 temporadas al vencer el jueves 8-2 a los Rojos de Cincinnati.
“Es algo muy importante. Creo que mucha gente piensa que es solo un rito de paso (pero) no es fácil”, declaró el mánager de los Dodgers Dave Roberts. “Así que es algo de lo que todos estamos muy orgullosos, pero entendemos claramente que ese no es el objetivo final”.
Los Dodgers (93-60) disputarán los playoffs por 14 temporada consecutiva, con lo que igualan el récord que los Bravos de Atlanta establecieron de 1991-2005.
“Es el primer paso”, dijo Mookie Betts mientras se secaba el champán de los ojos. “Nos queda un largo camino por recorrer”.
La celebración en el terreno de juego fue algo calmada tras el último out el jueves. Pero los jugadores se soltaron en el vestuario, donde el champán y la cerveza salpicaron desde el suelo hasta el techo.
“Creo que es una de esas situaciones en las que, como en el béisbol se juega a diario, los jugadores se centran en rendir”, dijo Roberts. “Así que no hay muchos momentos para celebrar. Por eso es agradable ver a los chicos soltarse un poco”.
A pesar de todos sus laureles, los Dodgers creen que todavía tienen algo que demostrar.
El año pasado, el equipo pulverizó el récord de gasto de las Grandes Ligas con una nómina total de 515 millones de dólares, dando alas a críticas de que tienen una supuesta ventaja injusta.
“Lo que estamos creando aquí es especial”, afirmó Max Muncy. “Definitivamente no se le da el reconocimiento que merece. Todo el mundo se fija en la nómina, pero nunca hablamos de cómo hacemos las cosas bien, de cómo nos preparamos adecuadamente o de cómo cuidamos todos esos pequeños detalles. De eso no se habla”.
Los bicampeones defensores de la Serie Mundial aún pujan por el primer puesto de preclasificación de la Liga Nacional, que actualmente está en posesión de los Cerveceros de Milwaukee. Los Ángeles comenzó el día con una ventaja de tres juegos y medio sobre los Bravos (89-64) por el segundo puesto, pero está por detrás de los Cerveceros (95-57).
“Seguimos luchando por uno de los dos primeros puestos”, dijo Roberts. “Creo que hacemos bien celebrando, pero sin dejar que eso afecte a lo que sigue. Tenemos que tomar el vuelo y jugar contra los Gigantes mañana”.
Los Dodgers buscan convertirse en el primer equipo en conquistar tres campeonatos consecutivos de la Serie Mundial desde que los Yankees lo lograron de 1998 a 2000.
Este es el cuarto título divisional asegurado más temprano para los Dodgers. Aseguraron el Oeste de la Liga Nacional el 10 de septiembre de 2019, el 13 de septiembre de 2022 y el 16 de septiembre de 2023.
Los Ángeles aprovechará ese tiempo para recuperar lesionados. Eso empieza con Shohei Ohtani.
El cuatro veces Jugador Más Valioso ha estado en la lista de lesionados de 15 días desde el 8 de septiembre por una inflamación en el bíceps derecho y les dijo a los reporteros a principios de este mes que ya no lanzará más en lo que resta de temporada. La estrella de dos vías hizo swings desde un tee por primera vez el martes y se sintió bien. Se espera que regrese como bateador antes de que termine la temporada regular, aunque no está claro si podrá llegar al 100% de salud antes de octubre.
Roki Sasaki, en la lista de lesionados por una ampolla en el dedo medio, lanzó en una práctica de bateo en vivo el miércoles en Cincinnati y salió bien. Roberts indicó que su próxima aparición será como abridor.
Blake Snell salió prematuramente de la apertura del miércoles después de un inning por rigidez en la ingle izquierda. Su situación es incierta.
Se espera que el cerrador puertorriqueño Edwin Díaz, quien ha estado en la lista de lesionados desde agosto por una inflamación en el cuello, sea activado el viernes. El venezolano Edgardo Henríquez, un preparador de mesa en el bullpeb, está en la lista de lesionados por molestias en la parte baja de la espalda. Se le realizó una resonancia magnética en Los Ángeles el miércoles, que reveló una distensión lumbar, y su rehabilitación se pausará por unos días.
El primera base Freddie Freeman, aquejado por dolor en la rodilla derecha, regresó a la alineación el martes y cortó una mala racha de 3 hits en 30 turnos con tres imparables. Sumó otros dos hits el jueves.
Los Dodgers protagonizaron el mayor impacto de la fecha límite de cambios al adquirir a Tarik Skubal, ganador en dos ocasiones del premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, procedente de los Tigres. Skubal tiene marca de 3-2 con efectividad de 2.52 en ocho aperturas con los Dodgers.
La incorporación de Skubal convirtió a los Dodgers en los grandes favoritos en las apuestas para ganar la Serie Mundial. Pero después de comenzar la temporada con marca de 61-36, los Dodgers tienen registro de 31-24 desde la pausa del Juego de Estrellas.
Los Dodgers dejaron a 12 corredores en base y se fueron de 0 en 11 con corredores en posición de anotar en la derrota del miércoles ante los Reds, algo que, según Roberts, necesita mejorar.
“Se trata de poder rematar a los equipos cuando tenemos oportunidades. En la postemporada no se presentan muchas oportunidades. Hay que saber aprovecharlas”, dijo Roberts.

Sin Shohei Ohtani, los Dodgers amarraron su quinto título divisional
El equipo angelino derrotó a los Cincinnati Reds y se colocó en una posición privilegiada
Los Angeles volvió a teñirse de fiesta al vencer 8-2 a los Cincinnati Reds. Con este triunfo, los Dodgers aseguraron su quinto título consecutivo de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional. La ofensiva brilló gracias a Kyle Tucker, quien pegó home run y produjo tres carreras, junto a cuadrangulares de Miguel Rojas y producciones de Freddie Freeman, Max Muncy y Josué De Paula.
La hazaña cobra un valor aún más especial por las complejas circunstancias que rodeaban al equipo en el terreno. La superestrella japonesa Shohei Ohtani tuvo que ver la celebración desde la banca, marginado del line up tras ingresar a la lista de lesionados por molestias físicas. Sin la imponente presencia de su bateador designado titular, la alineación angelina tuvo que reinventarse y responder con contundencia en el momento exacto.
Ante la ausencia del fenómeno japonés, la profundidad del plantel asumió la responsabilidad de dar la cara por el proyecto. Bateadores de experiencia y jugadores de rol enlazaron turnos de alta calidad para sostener a la ofensiva en los momentos más tensos de la jornada. Paralelamente, el pitcheo dictó cátedra desde la loma para silenciar los bates rivales y mantener el control del encuentro de principio a fin.
Al caer el último out de la tarde, el vestidor estalló en júbilo para dar inicio al ya tradicional baño de champán. Este quinto banderín divisional al hilo confirma la jerarquía de una organización construida para sobreponerse a cualquier adversidad. Con el billete a octubre garantizado, Los Angeles envía un mensaje contundente a toda la liga de cara a la postemporada.

Los Dodgers reconquistan el Oeste de la Liga Nacional y sellan su 14ª postemporada consecutiva
CINCINNATI._ Por más que intenten ver el 2026 como una temporada independiente, todo lo que los Dodgers han hecho este año es imposible de separar del contexto más amplio de lo que han logrado en más de una década de excelencia.
Catorce clasificaciones consecutivas a la postemporada. Cinco títulos divisionales seguidos. La inusual oportunidad de luchar por un tricampeonato de la Serie Mundial.
Los Dodgers alcanzaron otro hito importante en la defensa de su título al recuperar la corona del Oeste de la Liga Nacional con una victoria de 8-2 sobre los Rojos la tarde del jueves en el Great American Ball Park. Tres días después de su tradicional brindis con champaña para celebrar que aseguraron un lugar en la postemporada, conquistar el Oeste desató una eufórica celebración en el clubhouse, que esperan sea la primera de muchas durante las próximas semanas.
En sus 14 participaciones consecutivas en la postemporada, igualando un récord, los Dodgers han conquistado 13 títulos divisionales. El único equipo que logró destronarlos fueron los Gigantes del 2021, que los superaron por estrecho margen en una de las luchas por el Oeste de la Liga Nacional más reñidas de los últimos tiempos.
La ofensiva de los Dodgers, cuya inconsistencia ha sido una preocupación constante a lo largo de la temporada, brindó bastante respaldo desde temprano para apoyar un juego de bullpen programado. Kyle Tucker encabezó el ataque con cuatro hits y tres carreras impulsadas, quedándose a un triple de conseguir el primer ciclo de los Dodgers desde el 2017. Freddie Freeman, Max Muncy, el dominicano Josué De Paula y el venezolano Miguel Rojas también remolcaron anotaciones.
Justin Wrobleski abrió el juego de bullpen con tres innings perfectos, y aunque Blake Treinen permitió un jonrón solitario en el cuarto episodio, Landon Knack lanzó cuatro entradas en blanco antes de que Seth Halvorsen concediera una rayita en el noveno acto.
Con nueve juegos restantes en la temporada regular, los Dodgers están lejos de contar con todo su plantel. Su mejor bateador, Shohei Ohtani, está en la lista de lesionados de 15 días, al igual que el cubano Andy Pagés, llamado por primera vez al Juego de Estrellas. La rotación de seis abridores que utilizaron durante gran parte de la temporada se ha reducido a cuatro abridores completamente acondicionados en el róster activo, lo que hizo necesario recurrir a un juego de bullpen el jueves.
Los Dodgers esperan recuperar refuerzos antes de la postemporada y se beneficiarían enormemente de asegurar el descanso en la primera ronda para avanzar directamente a la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional, lo que les daría cinco días libres después del final de la temporada regular. Tienen una ventaja de 4.0 juegos sobre los Bravos por el segundo puesto de la Liga Nacional.
Esta versión de los Dodgers no está exenta de defectos, pero tampoco lo estuvieron los equipos campeones consecutivos del 2024 y 2025. Después de convertirse el año pasado en el primer equipo en un cuarto de siglo en defender con éxito su título, buscarán el primer tricampeonato de Grandes Ligas desde los Yanquis de 1998 al 2000.
“Tenemos tanta hambre como en el 2024 y 2025”, dijo el piloto Dave Roberts. “Esta es una temporada aparte. Nuestros muchachos lo entienden”.
(Con información de MLB)

CINCINNATI -- The Los Angeles Dodgers clinched their fifth consecutive NL West division title and 13th in the 14 seasons, sparked by four hits from Kyle Tucker that included a first-inning home run in an 8-2 win over the Cincinnati Reds on Thursday,
The two-time World Series champions already were assured of their 14th straight postseason appearance, trying the record Atlanta set from 1991 to 2005. Los Angeles (93-60) had clinched no worse than a wild-card berth on Monday.
Los Angeles opened a 9 1/2-game lead over second-place San Diego and has the second-best record in the NL as they try to overtake Milwaukee (95-57 entering Thursday) for the top NL seed. The division clinching was the fourth earliest for the Dodgers after Sept. 10 in 2019, Sept. 13 in 2022 and Sept. 16 in 2023.
Tucker fell a triple short of the cycle and had three RBIs, hitting a single and a pair of doubles. He hit his 16th homer, a two-run drive in the first off Brady Singer, who allowed seven runs, nine hits and four walks in 3 1/3 innings.
Freddie Freeman's sacrifice fly and Tucker's RBI double boosted the lead in the second, and the Dodgers opened a 7-0 lead in the fourth on Max Muncy's two-run double and Josue De Paula's RBI single.
Dodger left-hander Justin Wrobleski, making his 22nd start this season and first since Sept. 6, did not allow a baserunner in three innings while striking out three.
Wrobleski and Blake Treinen combined to retire their first 11 batters before Sal Stewart's 32nd homer.
Landon Knack (1-0) allowed four hits over four scoreless innings for his first big league win since May 31 last year.
Miguel Rojas homered off Brandon Williamson in the ninth.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said reliever Edwin Díaz (neck inflammation) finished his minor league injury rehabilitation assignment and will be activated this weekend.
Dodgers: RHP Tyler Glasnow (4-1, 3.50) starts Friday against San Francisco, who send LHP Cesar Perdomo (0-1, 3.68) to the mound,
Reds: RHP Chase Burns (15-3, 2.80) starts Friday against the Chicago Cubs.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Cincinnati Reds 8-2 on Thursday, September 17th, to clinch the National League West.
Kyle Tucker’s big day
Tucker has been fantastic lately, and Thursday’s game was a true cherry on top. He went 4-for-5 with two doubles, a home run, and a single, and drove in three runs.
Over the last seven games, Tucker has put up a .375/.467/.917 slash line with three home runs, nine RBIs, five walks, and three strikeouts.
Even over the last 15 games, Tucker is hitting .280/.383/.680 with five home runs and 11 RBIs.
Tucker nearly had a cycle, but when he gapped a ball in the eighth inning, he didn’t push for a triple and held up instead.
Still, this was Tucker’s game and a promising sign of things to come.
It was not just Tucker who played well, though; Freddie Freeman went 2-for-3 with an RBI and a walk, while Max Muncy went 2-for-4 with two RBIs.
Additionally, Miguel Rojas added the eighth run with a solo home run in the top of the ninth.
Considering the Dodgers went 0-for-11 with runners in scoring position on Wednesday, Thursday’s game was a welcome development.
Bullpen bounce-back
Justin Wrobleski looked great for three innings, allowing no hits and pitching them all perfect, with three strikeouts.
He was only at 32 pitches, and if Roberts wanted to stretch him out, he could have, but the Dodgers want to save his best stuff for the postseason.
Additionally, Landon Knack handled the bulk of the relief, allowing just four hits and recording two punchouts over four innings of clean work.
Blake Treinen and Seth Halvorsen each allowed a run, but thanks to Knack and Wrobleski, it was more than enough to finally clinch the division.

CINCINNATI — There is the road less traveled. And there is what the Dodgers do every year.
For the 13th time in the past 14 years, they are the National League West division champions. They clinched it with an 8-2 victory over the Cincinnati Reds Thursday afternoon.
The Dodgers scored seven times in the first four innings, leaving little doubt about the outcome.
There was little doubt about this year’s division title either.
The Dodgers spent a total of six days out of first place this season – two in April, four in May. They took over first place for good after beating the San Diego Padres on May 19. They had a double-digit lead for the first time on June 28 and have led by no less than seven games every day since.
Any drama is quickly draining from the playoff seeding race as well. Thursday’s win put the Dodgers four games up on the Atlanta Braves (off on Thursday) with a magic number of six to clinch one of the top two seeds and a first-round bye.
Clinching a postseason berth for the 14th consecutive season (tying the Braves’ MLB record) on Monday required only a champagne toast and a short speech from Dodgers manager Dave Roberts.
“This is kind of the expectation,” veteran Max Muncy said of that. “It’s not something you take for granted, but it’s the expectation that you can reach this point every single year.”
Clinching another division title, however, did not get the low-key treatment. The team celebrated in earnest.
No one had more reason to wash away the regular season and focus on the postseason than Kyle Tucker. The offseason’s big signing, Tucker has been a disappointment, making his four-year, $240 million contract stand out as the kind of mistake only the Dodgers could absorb.
But Tucker has shown signs of life recently.
He drove in the Dodgers’ first two runs Thursday with a first-inning home run, had an RBI double in the second inning, singled and scored a run in the fourth. With a shot at the cycle, he flew out in the fifth then doubled again in the eighth. Over his past eight games, Tucker is 12 for 29 (.414) with three doubles, a triple and four home runs.
Muncy had a two-run double in the fourth inning and Freddie Freeman went 2 for 3 with two runs scored and a sacrifice fly. Miguel Rojas hit a solo home run in the ninth.
The early lead made the bullpen game a smooth ride. Justin Wrobleski started and retired all nine batters he faced. Blake Treinen gave up a solo home run to Sal Stewart in the fourth inning. But Landon Knack followed that with four scoreless innings.

They hit their magic number, but minus the magic.
The Dodgers trudged toward October by clinching their 13th National League West title in 14 years on Thursday, their customary march mired in a quicksand of questions.
Has any Dodger team during this golden era entered the playoffs with more injuries, more uncertainty, and a greater fear of underachievement?
Will the party in Cincinnati be the last time they celebrate this season?
The magic is indeed missing, and after two seasons of conjuring up postseason greatness, these back-to-reality Dodgers appear headed for an early fall.
The Three-Peat looks like a no-go.
Despite the best efforts from baseball’s best braintrust, their latest creation simply doesn’t have the appearance of a championship team.
They’re aging, they’re hurting and, with only a couple of weeks left until the beginning of their annual autumnal angst, they look tired and taut and unprepared for this monumental tussle with history.
“I think for me, the message was, ‘We haven’t come close to playing our best baseball yet.’” manager Dave Roberts told reporters when relaying his speech to the team earlier this week upon clinching a record-tying 14th consecutive playoff berth.
He added, “The message was, we’ve accomplished a lot up to this point, all the while not playing our best baseball. So let’s get some of these guys healthy.”
Haven’t come close to playing our best baseball… Let’s get some of these guys healthy.
Not exactly “Win one for the Gipper” stuff, but completely accurate. These postseason’s themes are more realistic than inspirational, and for good reason.
No, they haven’t come close to playing their best baseball. Forget what you see in these season-ending games against some of the worst teams. Remember, instead, what they’ve done against some of baseball’s best.
Since the All-Star break, they are 4-12 against the five National League playoff contenders. The Atlanta Braves swept them. The Chicago Cubs swept them. The Milwaukee Brewers dominated them.
These teams will be waiting for them in October, and even baseball’s richest roster might not be enough to carry this staggered bunch through their toughest stretch. They’ve played a lot of games in three years, all under baseball’s brightest spotlight, every night, scores of media, millions of fans, a worldwide whirl for 28 regular dudes, and it’s finally taken its toll.
They’ve hit the wall… and the wall is about to hit back.
“It’s not easy, I think it’s a lot harder than people think it is,” said Roberts. “Human nature alone, when you’re hungry, when you’re chasing something, it’s a lot more easy to be motivated, versus, having been there, done that, it gets a little trite, a little old.”
He added: “To keep guys enthusiastic, focused, hungry, that’s harder. But to their credit, they stayed the course. And for me, we’re just as hungry as we were in ‘24 and ‘25. This is a separate season. Our guys understand.”
The 1988-89 Lakers understood, too. And they still got burned in ways that Dodger fans will find painfully familiar. Showtime was chasing the original “three-peat” trademarked by Pat Riley when the Lakers were swept by the Detroit Pistons in a Finals that seemed cursed,
Byron Scott missed the series with a hamstring injury and Magic Johnson essentially missed the final two games with a hamstring injury and they couldn’t survive.
This looks like the Dodgers today. Their injuries feel too major, and the impact too deep.
Start with Shohei Ohtani. The Dodgers haven’t won a full-season championship in 38 years without him at the top of the lineup. He’ll be there again, but his body has been breaking down for the last couple of months, and, before being recently placed on the injured list — finally! — he was only a shadow of himself.
He hasn’t hit a home run or driven in a run outside of Coors Field in more than a month. In his last 24 games before going on the IL with biceps and knee issues, he was batting .198. The Dodgers can’t admit it, and Ohtani would never acknowledge it, but this is a man in serious need of an extended rest.
Teoscar Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday in the Dodgers’ win against the Reds was his second home run in as many nights.
Also on the injured list in these final days is Andy Pages, who was having a career year before breaking his hand. He’ll return without much time to get ready for October, and this is a man who will need some time, as he has a career .114 average in the postseason and was even benched last year before he redeemed himself with that picturesque catch over Kiké Hernández.
Speaking of last October’s heroes, the biggest savior has also spent the summer in pain, Will Smith battling neck issues until recently returning to the lineup. But the comeback has been bumpy. In his initial games since returning at the start of September, Smith was batting .171. Last October he set a major league record by catching 73 innings in the World Series. He is still paying the price.
Then there’s Freddie Freeman, whose bat doesn’t have the same pop, who’s step doesn’t have the same spring, and who has his worst OPS in 14 years. Add an inconsistent Mookie Betts and an incredibly streaky Teoscar Hernández to an already-shaky lineup.
It’s been such an unsteady year, Andrew Friedman’s two big offseason acquisitions have been busts. Edwin Díaz has been terrible, and then injured, then terrible again. Kyle Tucker has been terrible, then worse, then mostly invisible.
Even the Dodgers two role-playing heroes have seemingly disappeared. Kiké Hernández, at age 35, has his lowest home-run total — three — in 12 years. Miguel Rojas, at age 37, has his lowest home run and RBI totals in nine years.
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
As if they didn’t have enough problems on the field and at the plate, check out the mound. No, don’t.
Even what should be their strength is now being threatened. Blake Snell left Wednesday’s game early with groin issues and Tyler Glasnow recently complained of general discomfort. This leaves a proven playoff rotation of two, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tarik Skubal, and if you think Yamamoto threw a lot of innings last October, this time he won’t be able to leave the mound for a month.
In all, this is a Dodger team facing its toughest challenge yet, their quest for an historic three-peat much tougher than the last two journeys, one that will require arguably the greatest stretch of baseball in franchise history to complete.
This division title is a nice beginning.
It could also be the end.

CINCINNATI — A few days off sounds pretty good right about now.
“I do think this team, as much as any team we’ve had, that week off is probably most beneficial,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said of locking down one of the top two seeds in the National League in order to get a first-round bye and five days off before starting the postseason.
Going into Thursday’s game, the Dodgers held a 3 ½-game lead over the Atlanta Braves for the second seed in the NL with a magic number of seven to clinch that first-round bye. The Dodgers trail the Milwaukee Brewers by three games for the top seed.
“It’s always helpful in the sense of giving your guys a break to reset,” Roberts said. “But given all the tax and where our guys are health-wise, to get that week would be huge.”
Blake Snell joined the long list of players with injury concerns when he left his start Wednesday after just one inning due to left groin tightness. The Dodgers also have questions about Shohei Ohtani (knee, biceps), Freddie Freeman (knee), Edgardo Henriquez (back), Andy Pages (hand), Roki Sasaki (blister) and Dalton Rushing (elbow).
Pages has been swinging a bat and hitting off the Trajekt machine this week, and it is “very likely” he will be activated from the IL during the homestand starting Friday, according to Roberts.
Ohtani has been “progressing” this week and is feeling “normal-ish” with no pain in his right arm or left knee, Roberts said.
“He’s doing everything he needs to do,” Roberts said. “I still don’t know when (his) time to return to play is. But everything that I hear is really positive.”
Snell could undergo an MRI to determine the severity of his groin injury. But he was optimistic after the game Wednesday that he had pulled back and left the game soon enough that it won’t be a serious issue and he might be able to make one more start before the end of the regular season.
“It’s all contingent on how he feels and potential imaging,” Roberts said. “It doesn’t make sense to just shut him down until the postseason if he can pitch. But again, if he’s not 100 percent to pitch, then we have no problem kicking the can.”
DIAZ RETURN
Right-hander Edwin Diaz completed his rehab assignment with Triple-A Oklahoma City on Wednesday and will join the Dodgers in Los Angeles this weekend with the expectation that he will be activated from the Injured List.
Diaz will be used in “low-leverage” situations, Roberts said, with a need to prove he can pitch well enough to assume a bigger role if he is on the postseason roster.
“I think, like anything, it should be a meritocracy,” Roberts said. “You have to earn the right of opportunities, but then you also have to perform, right? Eddie understands that. I think where we’re at now we just need guys to buy in, perform and go from there. That’s what he’s about.”
Roberts called Diaz’s final outing with OKC was “his best one yet.” Diaz pitched a scoreless inning, gave up a double and didn’t get a single swing-and-miss on any of 15 pitches.
“Quality of strike-throwing. Get guys out,” Roberts said of what he hopes to see from Diaz. “That’s probably it. As you get into the postseason, every inning’s leverage. So that’s kind of it. Quality of strike-throwing, and get guys out.”
UP NEXT
Giants (LHP Cesar Perdomo, 0-1, 3.68 ERA) at Dodgers (RHP Tyler Glasnow, 4-1, 3.50 ERA), Friday, 7:10 p.m., Apple TV, 570 AM

The Los Angeles Dodgers brought third baseman Max Muncy and outfielder Josue De Paula back into the lineup for Thursday’s series finale against the Cincinnati Reds.
The Dodgers lost Wednesday’s game after Cy Young winner Blake Snell went down with a groin injury after pitching just one inning. Luckily, Snell believes he can still make a start before the end of the regular season, which ends in less than two weeks.
LA won the first two games of the series, shutting down a powerful Reds lineup, and will look to do the same to win the series Wednesday.
Who is Starting for the Dodgers?
Justin Wrobleski will start for the Dodgers on Wednesday, making his 25th appearance of the regular season. Two of his last three appearances have come out of the bullpen, and none of them have lasted more than three innings since his return from the injured list with a forearm problem.
He has a 3.78 ERA on the year, striking out 111 batters over the course of 133.1 innings—his heaviest workload in an MLB season so far.
How deep into the game he goes depends on him, but the Dodgers will have backup in the form of Landon Knack whenever Wrobleski is ready to come out.
Who is in the Dodgers’ Lineup?
The Dodgers still don’t have Shohei Ohtani in the lineup, but Tommy Edman has replaced him well and will play center field on Thursday. Freddie Freeman moves up a couple of spots into the No. 2 hole, followed by right fielder Kyle Tucker, who will bat third.
Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez takes over the cleanup spot, followed by Muncy, who slides back into third base and bats fifth. De Paula serves as the designated hitter and will bat sixth, with catcher Hunter Feduccia giving Will Smith an off day in the No. 7 spot.
Second baseman Alex Freeland will bat eight for the Dodgers, with Miguel Rojas rounding out the lineup and playing shortstop—giving Mookie Betts a well-deserved rest day.

Who is Starting for the Reds?
Veteran right-hander Brady Singer is starting for the Reds, making his 30th appearance of the season. He has reached that mark in each of the last three seasons, and has 25 or more appearances in all seven of his MLB campaigns bar 2020.
He isn’t having the best year despite his regular consistency, though, as he has a 5.38 ERA through 150.2 innings with only 125 strikeouts on the season.
Singer didn’t face the Dodgers in last week’s series in Los Angeles, but he has a pretty good track record against the team. In three appearances against LA, all of which came during his time with Kansas City, he has a 1.89 ERA through 19 innings with 15 strikeouts.
The Dodgers will hope to break that trend on Thursday as they look to bring themselves even closer to a first-round postseason bye. The first pitch of Thursday’s game comes at 9:40 p.m. PT.

Los Angeles Dodgers star Kyle Tucker may be getting hot just in time for the playoffs.
The National League West-leading Dodgers (90-57) will look to extend their winning streak to nine games when they visit the Miami Marlins (72-76) on Saturday. The Marlins, in turn, have lost seven of their past eight games.
Tucker went 3-for-3 with a season-high five RBIs in Los Angeles’ 6-2 victory over Miami on Friday. He fell a double short of the cycle.
Entering Friday, Tucker was on pace for his fourth straight month with an OPS at or below .700, and that’s not what the Dodgers thought they were getting when they signed him to a four-year, $240 million contract in January.
Tucker, who has posted OPS numbers of .993 and .841 over the past two years, impressed Marlins manager Clayton McCullough with his performance on Friday.
“Independent of how this season has gone, (Tucker) is still a terrific hitter,” McCullough said. “He handles lefties well. He got a hanging breaking ball and turned the game for them.”
Tucker produced five straight seasons with more than 20 homers before mustering just 14 in 2026. But if he can finish strong, that will help a Dodgers squad that is missing injured sluggers Shohei Ohtani (right biceps inflammation), Freddie Freeman (right knee) and Andy Pages (left hand). Those three players have hit a combined 67 homers this season.
Los Angeles also saw Josue De Paula make his MLB debut on Friday. De Paula went 0-for-3 with a walk after tearing up Double-A pitching.
“We want to get him some major-league at-bats to see what it looks like,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
The Dodgers will turn to right-hander Tyler Glasnow (4-0, 3.12 ERA) to make the start on Saturday.
His per-nine-innings averages are outstanding in terms of hits allowed (5.3), walks (2.7) and strikeouts (10.9). The Dodgers are 8-2 when he starts, and this will be his fourth start since coming back from a near-three-month injury absence.
Glasnow is 1-1 with a 3.86 ERA in five career starts versus the Marlins.
Miami will counter with right-hander Tyler Phillips (5-6, 3.51), who is 1-0 with a 6.94 ERA in six career appearances (one start) against the Dodgers.
For his career overall, Phillips has a sterling 2.49 ERA in 71 relief appearances, but a 5.13 ERA in 25 career starts.
As for Miami’s offense, the Marlins are hoping that shortstop Otto Lopez is back on track after a 4-for-5 performance on Friday.
This year, Lopez hit .322 in March/April; .339 in May; and .340 in June. That hot start made him a first-time All-Star. However, he batted .284 in July and just .236 in August.
Thanks to Friday’s big game, he is now hitting .342 in September.
“After the phenomenal first half, he struggled for a bit,” McCullough said. “He looks to be back in a good spot, hitting the ball to all fields. It’s something we have grown accustomed to, and it bodes well for us to have him get hits in bunches.”
–Field Level Media

Shohei Ohtani’s aching right arm. Freddie Freeman’s throbbing right knee. Edwin Díaz’s disastrous form on a minor-league rehabilitation assignment.
Whatever problems surfaced in recent weeks, the Dodgers were able to convince themselves they could overcome them.
The reason: Even with Ohtani unable to pitch, they had the most talented starting rotation of this era.
Suddenly, that source of comfort is a major concern.
Blake Snell departed his start in Cincinnati on Wednesday after just one inning with what was described as a tight left groin.
Consider that Tyler Glasnow traveled directly home from Miami rather than to follow the Dodgers to Great American Ball Park for their four-game series against the Reds, and there are reasons to be worried.
Very worried.
With an inconsistent offense and combustible bullpen, the Dodgers were going to be heavily dependent on their starting pitching in the playoffs.
That rotation could now be unraveling.

The last time Snell strained his left groin was when he was pitching for the San Francisco Giants in 2024. He was sidelined for a month.
For what it’s worth, Snell is convinced this particular injury isn’t severe and plans to make his next start, according to people familiar with this situation.
“Stopped before it got too bad,” one of the people said.
Then again, weren’t similar claims once made about Ohtani?
As for Glasnow, he remains on track to pitch on Friday.
Manager Dave Roberts said Glasnow skipped the Cincinnati leg of the trip to better prepare for his starting assignment at Dodger Stadium against the San Francisco Giants.
“Get him acclimated to Pacific Standard Time,” Roberts said.
By sending Glasnow back to Los Angeles, the Dodgers spared him a three-hour flight from Miami to Cincinnati.
Glasnow was sidelined for 3 ½ months because of back problems, and Roberts intimated something could be wrong with him after his most recent start. In his last two appearances, the 6-foot-8 right-hander gave up a combined eight runs, 11 hits and seven walks in 10 innings.
The questions about Snell’s and Glasnow’s health came at a time when the rotation was coming together before the postseason.
Snell in particular was sharp after returning from an elbow cleanup that cost him three months. Before his early departure on Wednesday, Snell was 4-0 with a 1.04 earned-run average since he was activated from the injured list on Aug. 11.
Snell wasn’t the only Cy Young Award-caliber pitcher rounding into shape.
The day before Snell scaled the mound, it was Yamamoto’s turn to do so, and last year’s World Series Most Valuable Player pitched seven scoreless innings in a 4-0 win over the Reds.
The seven-inning start was the third in a row for Yamamoto, who improved his record to 14-8 and lowered his earned-run average to 2.51.
“I feel really good and I don’t have any physical problems,” Yamamoto told reporters in Japanese. “I want to treat practice each and every day with importance and go into October in the best condition.”
The opening game of the series was started by Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young Award winner who was acquired from the Detroit Tigers before the trade deadline.
Skubal pitched seven scoreless innings of his own in a 4-1 victory over the Reds. In his previous start, which was also against the Reds but at Dodger Stadium, Skubal pitched 7 ⅓ innings.
“Just getting in a rhythm,” Skubal said.
Just last week, the Dodgers had a playoff rotation that would have looked to other teams like the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse.
Now, there’s a chance they could be forced to send Roki Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan to the mound in playoff games.
The Dodgers could conceivably win a championship with a rotation of Yamamoto, Skubal, Sasaki and Sheehan but that would require their offense to be productive.
How much can the Dodgers count on that, considering the physical problems Ohtani and Freeman have encountered? And how would using Sasaki as a starter instead of a reliever affect their bullpen?
Snell removed himself from his start on Wednesday so the Dodgers wouldn’t have to find out. The question is whether he did so in time. Their season depends on it.

On Tuesday night, the Los Angeles Dodgers continued their series with the Cincinnati Reds in Ohio.
The Dodgers won by a score of 4-0.
Freddie Freeman finished with three hits in five at-bats.
Freeman Makes Statement After Game
After the game, Freeman met with the media (via SportsNet LA).
The future Hall of Famer had recently missed several games due to injury.
That said, Freeman appears to be feeling fine.
Reporter: “Freddie, you had those three hits tonight. I know it’s kind of been back and forth for you dealing with this tendinitis, but how is your knee feeling right now, and how good was it to see the results fall today?”
Freeman: “No, it was good. I’ve been kind of working a new thing in the cage the last couple days, so I got to go for results-based things right now. We got to get hot with two weeks to go, and looking to be hot for a few weeks, that’s all I’m trying to do. So I felt good in the cage today, and luckily was able to throw some seeing-eye bleeders out there today.”
Reporter: “With your knee though, are you finding that you still want to give it some time here and there, or is it feeling significantly better?”
Freeman: “I was supposed to be off tomorrow, but I played myself in there. So I’m very excited, I’m in there tomorrow. I think they were trying to manage it. I told them I was good to be able to play every day, but they’re trying to be mindful. I feel good, I had no pain in the knee today. So with three hits today, I got myself in there tomorrow.”
Looking At Freeman Right Now
Freeman was picked in the 2nd round of the 2007 MLB Draft.
He is in the middle of his 5th season with the Dodgers.
Prior to Los Angeles, the ten-time MLB All-Star had a 12-year run with the Atlanta Braves.
Right now, Freeman is batting .296 with 159 hits, 16 home runs, 66 RBIs, 72 runs and seven stolen bases in 143 games.

Teoscar Hernández Is Delivering When The Dodgers Need Him The Most
LOS ANGELES — During a months-long spiral at the plate, Teoscar Hernández tried to maintain his upbeat, convivial persona.
But for much of the summer, before his September revival, it was difficult for the Dodgers’ fun-loving, seed-tossing veteran presence to look or feel like himself.
"I try to stay positive and bring the same energy that you guys know and see everyday — smiling, making jokes," Hernández told me. "But at the same time, it’s really hard."
(Photo by David Jordan/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts noticed his typically jovial outfielder looking a bit more sullen at times, too. It was understandable.
Hernández, a fixture in the Dodgers’ lineup whose clutch hitting, encouraging nature and penchant for performing on the sport’s biggest stage helped his team win back-to-back World Series titles, had a respectable .785 OPS when he went on the injured list on May 29 with a left hamstring strain.
But the 33-year-old did not look the same when he returned a month later. From June 29 to Aug. 29, his .592 OPS was the ninth-lowest mark among all qualified MLB hitters over that stretch.
"Some of the joy was sucked out," Roberts told me, "because it’s hard to be so joyful when you’re not performing. He was still a good teammate, always a good teammate, but I know there were a lot of frustrating moments for him."
Hernández’s struggles were compounded by the fact that the Dodgers were also getting little from their other corner outfielder, Kyle Tucker, or the rest of an offense that looked lifeless for much of the summer.
But now, at a crucial juncture for his team with All-Stars Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages sidelined, another All-Star in Freddie Freeman battling knee soreness and the playoffs just weeks away, Hernández is taking his frustration out constructively.
He is annihilating the baseball in September, leaving his summer slump behind and giving the Dodgers reason to believe in the depth of their offense again.
"When he catches fire," Dodgers infielder Tommy Edman said, "he’s as good as anybody in the game."
Even among Hernández’s best career stretches, the tear he’s on now stands out. Every part of his offensive profile is enhanced.
Hernández, who’s prone to swing and miss even when he’s going right, is making better swing decisions. From last month to this month, he has lowered his chase rate from 36.7% to 24.8%, tripled his walk rate from 4.3% to 15.1% and cut his strikeout rate nearly in half from 31.2% to 18.9%.
And along with a more selective approach, he is punishing every mistake in a way he couldn’t earlier this season.
Hernández’s hard-hit rate has skyrocketed from 34.5% in July to 47.5% in August to 60% this month. His average exit velocity this September (96.6 mph) is the highest of any month in his career.
Eight of his 10 hardest-hit balls this season have come in the last two weeks, and his power is being generated by the highest average bat speed he has produced in any month over the last two seasons (74.1 mph).
It’s a far cry from where Hernández was just a couple of weeks ago, when his year-long struggle against right-handers had the Dodgers considering using a platoon in left field. That no longer appears to be a consideration.
"Right now," Roberts said, "it’s just night and day."
So how, exactly, did Hernández find his way back?
"The most important part, he’s healthy," Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas told me. "If he’s healthy, we can see the Teo that’s running hard on the bases, stealing bases, going first to third. Obviously the bat is there because it’s his best tool, but seeing the complete player now is really refreshing."
Earlier this season, Hernández’s downturn looked familiar.
A year ago, he had the highest batting average on the team when he went on the IL in May with an adductor strain. He returned two weeks later, then watched his OPS precipitously drop 200 points from May 21 (.927) to July 21 (.727).
Clearly, the lower-body injury had lingered, throwing off his swing and sapping his power.
This year, it was happening again, only with his hamstring. The swing that worked for him before the injury was putting too much pressure on his lower half. Upon his return from the IL, he had a .562 OPS overall in July and a team-worst .496 OPS against right-handed pitching in August.
"I told Dave, ‘If you feel like you have to use somebody else in there, just do it,’" Hernández said.
(Photo by Meg Oliphant/Getty Images)
That would not be necessary. At least, not again after Aug. 25. The decision to sit him that day was noteworthy, considering the Dodgers were coming off an off day and facing a Braves team they were battling for a first-round bye.
In hindsight, it might have served as a wake-up call.
On Aug. 26, Hernández returned to the lineup in Atlanta with a two-hit day. He then ended the Dodgers’ next series in Detroit with a two-run homer off Framber Valdez, which might have been the turning point.
"I think that at-bat gave him the extra life that he needed for the last part of the season," Rojas said. "Obviously, baseball is about confidence, and you find confidence with success, and I thought that’s what he needed. He needed, like, one good swing that he knows he’s back, and then all of a sudden we see the results we get now."
There’s also a mechanical component to Hernández’s upswing.
Too often, Hernández felt both rushed and late at the plate as he worked his way back from his hamstring injury. He has since opened his stance in an effort, he says, to slow his body up, prevent his front hip from flying open and give him more time to see the ball. He has also traded his more subtle toe tap for a slightly more exaggerated leg lift and hip twist as a timing mechanism that seems to be producing more power.
These were moves he used before in his career. Now healthy, he feels his body can withstand the added force once again.
Sometimes with hitting, the littlest tweaks can yield the biggest results.
"That’s why it’s hard," Hernández told me. "One day, you don’t know what you’re doing. The next day, you change barely — sometimes it’s your hands, sometimes it’s your legs, sometimes it’s how low, how tall [in the stance] — and it can click, and you go on a heater."
Even compared to heaters of the past, though, this one is unlike most for Hernández. If September ended today, his 1.211 OPS this month would be the highest mark in any month of his career.
Hernández maintains that his confidence never wavered through the rough patch; that he knew, at some point, things would turn. His teammates shared that belief.
This was the same guy, after all, who homered in every playoff series last season.
(Photo by Melina Pizano/Getty Images)
"The clutch gene and everything that he has in him, the reason why we got him and the reason why we’ve been so good with him in the lineup the last couple years, nothing changed this year just because of a bad stretch," Rojas told me. "To be honest with you, I was never concerned about it … I want nobody in a big at-bat more than Teo."
After the big hit last month in Detroit, Hernández returned home, made the swing changes and provided the elusive clutch hit the scuffling Dodgers’ offense had been missing with a walk-off double to salvage a series against the Cardinals.
That hit helped spark an eight-game winning streak for the Dodgers, who started to look like themselves again.
Their ebullient left fielder is looking that way, too.
"I feel really good right now," Hernández said. "I’ve been working really hard for this, and I’m glad and happy that everything is coming together."

The Dodgers took Monday's series opener, 4-1, behind seven shutout innings from Tarik Skubal. Then, they won Tuesday's game, 4-0, behind seven shutout innings from Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
On Wednesday, LA has another superstar pitcher on the mound in left-hander Blake Snell.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going [Wednesday] — you feel good about preventing runs,” manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
Dodgers vs Reds Pitching Matchup on Wednesday
Snell is looking to continue his run of dominance since returning from midseason elbow surgery.
The left-hander has gone 4-0 with a 1.04 ERA across six starts, striking out 46 while allowing zero home runs over 34.2 innings of work.
Snell, who pitched 5.2 innings in his most recent start, is still looking to go deeper into games moving forward. He hasn't pitched more than six innings in any of his six starts.
“I mean the goal, at worst is definitely six for me,” Snell said. “I also know that I can go seven, eight, nine. I know I’m able to do it. So for me not to, I just have to get more efficient early in the game. I feel like once I get past the first couple innings, I start cruising and start figuring it out."
Opposite Snell will be left-hander Andrew Abbott, who's 6-11 with a 4.78 ERA and 120 strikeouts over 154.1 innings this season.

item.content:encoded:
gambit – noun
a chess opening in which a player risks one or more pawns or a minor piece to gain an advantage in position
Now, if your mind immediately went to the Marvel Comics character and you were confused, fair enough. Here's the clip you likely thought of, so we can all feel better and get to the heart of the essay.
And for the record, Freddie Freeman is hardly a minor piece, but giving up a major piece for tactical advantage is called a sacrifice, which wouldn't be appropriate given the circumstances here, as Freeman returned to the lineup for the September 15 game against the Cincinnati Reds.
A funny thought occurred to me while watching Freddie Freeman these last few months:
"Where did his power go? He sure seems like he's hitting into more double plays than I remember."
Looking at Freeman's stats for the year, apart from the power and RBI numbers being down a bit, nothing looks amiss. Honestly, I originally dismissed the feeling that something was wrong because Freeman was hitting up a storm for about a month after the All-Star Break.
There wasn't much power behind it, but when someone has a slash line of .367/.402/.411 over 24 games starting from the All-Star Break, pointing out fault feels like searching for a fly in the ointment. Yes, Freeman only had four doubles, eight RBIs, and nearly three times as many strikeouts as walks, but the overall body of work looked pretty good.
Freeman had a solid couple of games in Denver where he hit for doubles power and used the entire field. However, since the Denver series, where Freeman was hitting for average, he's just not.
When you aren't hitting for either average or power, alarm bells tend to finally ring.
Power drained
On September 9, Freeman was kept out of the lineup for right knee soreness and was considered day-to-day. To his credit, Dave Roberts did mention Freeman's slump on September 9.
Roberts said there was no one incident that caused Freeman's knee soreness, but he believes it has impacted his performance at the plate lately.
"Freddie does a really good job of hitting against his front side, and then when you can't do that with your front side, your right knee, then you're compromised," Roberts said. "I see there's a lot more swing-and-miss the last few days. That's just not who he is."
In the 18 games since the Colorado series until the start of play on September 15, Freeman has a slash line of .215/.338/.292. He does have his only home run of the second half, and his strikeouts-to-walk ratio is about 1.5/1 instead of 3/1 earlier in the year.
The problem is more of the eye test: Freeman is starting to finally look, and maybe move, like his age.
The splits on Baseball Savant from last year to now tell a pretty glaring tale: if you want to beat Freeman in 2026, go low and in. Also, Freeman feasted on center-cut pitches last year, not so this year.
I'm not a hitting expert, but having a diminished knee would make it harder to rotate to hit stuff middle in. On the September 13 broadcast of the finale against the Miami Marlins, Dontrelle Willis pointed out how Freeman is compromised rotationally generally, as pitches he would normally drive the other way are being weakly hit.
Even after Freeman hit a career-high and now league-high in double plays on Sunday, the Dodgers are not seriously entertaining putting Freeman on the injured list, per Katie Woo of The Athletic:
"I think it's one of those things where we've got to manage it … just pick spots to give him an off day here or there," Roberts said. "Again, we've just got to make sure he's at optimal health when we finish the season. So I think that he might not love it, but giving him a day off here or there might be beneficial."
The Dodgers don't believe an IL stint is necessary. Instead, Roberts is working in frequent off days. That's rare for Freeman, who hasn't played in fewer than 147 games in any season as a Dodger. Freeman had a scheduled day off over the Dodgers' previous nine-game homestand and also served as the designated hitter twice in that span. He wasn't in the lineup in the last game of the homestand on Wednesday, and following a team travel day, he also sat out Friday's game.
[Emphasis added.]
Freeman insists he feels fine.
Freeman hitting into two double plays and having a key miscue that contributed to the season and series loss to the Miami Marlins seems to indicate otherwise. It's worth noting that Freeman hit another tailor-made ground ball to second on a pitcher's pitch in his final at-bat that likely would have turned into another double play had Mookie Betts not doubled earlier in the frame.
"Just talking to him today, he said he felt good," Roberts said. "Obviously, the swings don't indicate that, don't validate that. On the defense, he's obviously not moving as well as he's used to.
"I think that he's doing anything and everything he can to prepare. But yeah, the last week, it's pretty obvious that he's not himself in the box."
Freeman won't be in Monday's starting lineup, Roberts said, but should play Tuesday…
[Emphasis added.]
Much like the sense one had when watching the Americanized remake of the original 1954 classic Gojira, Godzilla: King of the Monsters, one would expect a sense of deja vu right now, even with character actor Raymond Burr long dead.
Japanese Original, American Remake
I am typically not one to mince words, and I shall not do so here. Along with Dustin Nosler of Dodgers Digest, I was dead on the money regarding the Dodgers' malpractice in not acting decisively on Ohtani and his reluctance to admit injury in the face of personal dogma of success.
I argued that the Dodgers had bungled spectacularly, and events worked themselves out to prove my initial hypothesis correct on all fronts. Now the team has backed itself into a corner regarding Ohtani.
Contrary to what some might think, I did not enjoy being right. Frankly, I am correct often enough that I do not need the constant validation, unless it comes from either the Dodgers broadcast team or national media. (In which case, gimme.)
On September 11, Katie Woo of The Athletic wrote an op-ed recently that pulled few punches:
Nobody is blameless in the Shohei Ohtani injury saga. Not the Los Angeles Dodgers' front office, which should have been more proactive in protecting the team's biggest star. Not Ohtani, who downplayed the severity of his symptoms. And while hindsight is always 20-20, there were warning signs throughout the last few weeks that suggested a stint on the injured list was the safest course of action if the organization wanted to give its prized star the best possible chance at healing in time to begin the Dodgers' quest to win three straight World Series.
As the Dodgers prepare to be without Ohtani until Sept. 23 at the earliest, their biggest concern has become a reality. When Ohtani — who is expected to be placed on the injured list on Friday — does return, there is no guarantee he'll be in optimal condition for the postseason.
[Emphasis added.]
Um, excuse me? To quote one of the finest bits of media from the 2010s, I get to channel Chris Taylor for once and declare the following:
I know, Ms. Woo means nobody relevant, but words matter, and any excuse for referential comedy is a good one.
"I think that if it were a postseason game tomorrow, (Ohtani) would be in the lineup," manager Dave Roberts said Wednesday afternoon, hours before announcing Ohtani would be placed on the IL. "I think that now you're talking about two weeks, 14 days. I feel that that's substantial. He'll be in a much better place than he was today. Is it going to be to 100 percent? Probably not. But I do think that with this time that we're taking now he'll be in an adequate spot to finish the season."
Adequate is a far cry from healthy. It is fair to question how Ohtani was handled in the second half. Should he have attempted a pitching comeback, knowing his physical health was limited? Should the Dodgers have stopped that push sooner, or placed him on the injured list earlier? In their first season of managing Ohtani as a full-season two-way player, there was always going to be some trial and error. That was acknowledged from the start of the season by both Roberts and president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman. And in fairness, there was a cognizant effort to keep Ohtani as rested as possible, including a season-long six-man rotation and an attempt to maneuver Ohtani's starts to line up on games prior to a team off day, when possible.
Hindsight is generally 20/20. I am sure if the Dodgers were armed with foreknowledge in a do-over, they would not have Ohtani's best pitching starts of the year be in Houston and San Francisco … in May.
At the risk of retreading previously covered ground, we shall conclude this portion with Roberts' regret, especially considering that Ohtani tweaked his arm in his last played game and did not immediately tell anyone about it:
Looking back, it is something Roberts wish happened a week ago.
"I think if we look right now, here today, I would love to go back and put him on the IL," the manager said. "But I did feel at that moment in time, we all felt that giving him four days was sufficient. He was agreeable. Getting him out there on Monday with the hope that he would be able to play tonight. But where we're at right now, sure."
The Dodgers should have followed their own advice or learned from their handling of Ohtani to send Freeman back to Los Angeles for ten days before arriving in Cincinnati.
They didn't.
The Dodgers have calculated that whatever value Freeman can generate in the waning days of the season is greater than the potential benefit of having Freeman recuperate for ten days, having three days against the already-eliminated San Francisco Giants to use as a tune-up. Hence, the title of this essay: the Freeman Gambit.
Yesterday's game showed promise, even with a couple of moments that made one grimace. Freeman talked about how his three-hit performance likely ensured he would play on September 16.
Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic reported Roberts' comments on the health issues of players like Ohtani, Freeman, and Edgardo Henriquez after the Dodgers clinched their fourteenth consecutive postseason appearance:
"I think right now it's front of mind, it's not great," Roberts said. "But I will say this: Once you get to October, athletes have a magical way of feeling better. It happens every single year, where there's that extra adrenaline that athletes get when you get to the postseason."
The Dodgers still boast what is likely baseball's most talented roster and an established track record of postseason success that might be enough to make history. That was the heart of Roberts' toast: that the Dodgers have not yet played their best baseball.
They still can.
"We just haven't really gotten everyone all synced up at the same time," Muncy said. "So it is a scary thought to think what we could possibly do if we did that. So hopefully that's still ahead for us at the right time."
Whether the Freeman Gambit pays off over the next two weeks before the upcoming postseason tournament is an open question. Gambits are risky, even when they work.

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers will be in every game they play in October, and that alone means they will enter the playoffs as the favorites to win the World Series.
Not because of Shohei Ohtani. Not because of Freddie Freeman. And certainly not because of their bullpen.
There were a number of alarming developments in the last week or so, but if any team is designed to survive them, it’s the Dodgers.
Whatever their problems, they still have the best rotation in baseball.
No player influences the outcome of a game as much as a starting pitcher, and the Dodgers are the only team that will be able to roll out one Cy Young Award-caliber arm after another after another.
The Dodgers were negligent with Ohtani, and the verdict on their management of Freeman is pending, but they at least set up their pitchers the right way.
The rotation is more than a collection of big names. In Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell, the Dodgers have three starters who are peaking in time to deliver the kinds of performances that will be required for them to win their third consecutive World Series.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto pitched seven shutout innings on Tuesday in a 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds, marking his third consecutive seven-inning start.
“I feel really good and I don’t have any physical problems,” Yamamoto told reporters in Japanese. “I want to treat practice each and every day with importance and go into October in the best condition.”
Yamamoto isn’t alone.
The day before Yamamoto’s start, Tarik Skubal pitched seven scoreless innings of his own in a 4-1 victory over the Reds. In his previous start, which was also against the Reds but at Dodger Stadium, Skubal pitched 7 ⅓ innings.
“Just getting in a rhythm,” Skubal said.
Blake Snell, who is scheduled to take his turn in the rotation on Wednesday, was 4-0 with a 1.04 earned-run average in the six games he started since returning from an elbow cleanup that cost him three months.
The one source of concern in the rotation is Tyler Glasnow, who, like Snell, was slow-played in his return from an injury. Sidelined for 3 ½ months because of back problems, Glasnow showed promise in his first couple of starts after he came back. But in his last two starts, he gave up a combined eight runs, 11 hits and seven walks in 10 innings. But as the team’s No. 4 starter, he is unlikely to start more than one game in any postseason series.
Even before Ohtani was placed on the injured list because of right arm and left knee injuries, the starting pitching was likely going to have to carry the Dodgers – much as it did last year.
Recent developments have shifted even more of the burden to the starting pitchers.
Edwin Diaz, their $69-million closer, was blow-torched for five runs in ⅔ of an inning in the most recent game of his minor-league rehabilitation assignment. At this point, he’s a longshot to make the postseason roster.
Diaz’s failure to rediscover his All-Star form will have major ramifications on the bullpen, which lost ninth-inning candidate Edgardo Henriquez to a lower-back problem for the remainder of the regular season. Henriquez’s status for the playoffs remains a mystery.
Manager Dave Roberts’ current ninth-inning choice, Tanner Scott, is in a minor slump, as he has given up runs in five of his last 12 apperances.
While the Dodgers will have to find a closer – Roki Sasaki? – their ability to create favorable matchups in the innings before the ninth is also under question. The simplest way to address those uncertainties will be for the starters to pitch deeper into games. Last year, Yamamoto pitched a complete game in the National League Championship Series and another in his next start in the World Series. Snell had an eight-inning start in the NLCS.
The greater problem could be the already-inconsistent offense, which could go into the playoffs with physically-compromised versions of Ohtani and Freeman.
Freeman missed three of five games before starting at first base on Tuesday. Freeman collected three hits in the game, but he’s 37 years old and the Dodgers can’t be certain how his right knee will hold up.
As for Ohtani, Roberts reported on Tuesday that he resumed baseball activities. Roberts said he expected Ohtani to return before the end of the regular season, but hedged his prediction.
“Whether it happens or not,” Roberts said, “is to be determined.”
If the Dodgers don’t know if Ohtani will be able to even step into the batter’s box next week, how could they possibly count on him to be a consistent source of offense?
They can’t.
In other words, the margin for error could be miniscule for the Dodgers. Their starting pitchers might have to be close to perfect. The challenge will be formidable. But considering who will be pitching for them, it will be very much in the realm of possibility.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have allowed Freddie Freeman to play through a right knee injury as of late, while occasionally taking him out of the lineup when they see fit.
The Dodgers took a similar approach with Shohei Ohtani’s various ailments, but the team has been slightly more willing to rest Freeman compared to the four-time MVP.
Given the way Ohtani’s health regressed while continuing to play through injury, it begs the question of whether the Dodgers are making the same mistake with Freeman.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts acknowledged the concern over the weekend, but believes Freeman’s situation is different and does not necessitate a trip to the injured list.
“I think that’s certainly a valid question,” Roberts said on SportsNet LA. “I just think that right now with where we’re at in the season, an IL is not an option in the sense of I personally don’t think we have a better option. So I don’t think it needs to be 10 days, but could it be more than one?
“That’s a fair question. I’ve got to talk to the training staff, Freddie, and ultimately make that decision. But I don’t think an IL makes sense at all.”
Both Roberts and Freeman previously confirmed the knee injury is affecting the 37-year-old at the plate and in the field. The good news is that resting Freeman for just a couple of days has proven to reduce the severity of discomfort.
The Dodgers are not concerned with the injury getting worse, but they will continue to monitor his condition to make sure that remains the case. Before Tuesday’s game, Roberts said he would be watching each of Freeman’s at-bats closely to evaluate his right knee.
Freeman said his knee felt better heading into Tuesday’s contest after missing Monday’s game.
“Feels better today than he did yesterday, which is a good thing. I’ll re-evaluate after tonight,” Roberts began. “But obviously, there’s a day game on Thursday, so just kind of being mindful because I want him in that game on Thursday. I’ll be watching him closely.”
Dodgers need Freddie Freeman down the stretch
The Dodgers still have plenty to play for this season after clinching their 14th consecutive playoff berth.
L.A. is also closing in on another National League West title, but they still have work to do to clinch a top-two seed in the National League. Securing a first-round bye would be significant for the Dodgers, given the current injuries to Ohtani, Freeman and others.

Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman has been battling right knee pain, but the worst of it may be behind the team’s contact specialist.
Entering Tuesday’s game, Freeman was on a 3-for-30 cold streak and had missed three of the last six games because of his knee issue.
Things looked shaky for Freeman, who has built a reputation as one of baseball’s most consistent players.
However, he put together his best game in weeks, going 3-for-5 on singles, but showing the elite bat-to-ball skills that make him a candidate to bat around .300 year in, year out.
After the game, manager Dave Roberts noted that Freeman looked more like himself.
“It looked good,” Roberts said. “It looked more like Freddie.”
Freeman had asked Roberts before the game, jokingly, if he could play on Wednesday, a scheduled day off, if he got three hits.
As a result of Freeman’s performance, the manager is allowing Freeman to skip an off-day on Wednesday and play again, with the infielder eager to get the ball rolling.
“I feel like my faults are I try to hit the ball to the opposite field too much, and I let the ball get too deep,” he said.
“So today was [get the] foot down early, catch the ball out front a little bit, and it kind of worked. I wasn’t squaring the ball up in the game, but I’ll take those three hits and keep that work going tomorrow, and hopefully we’ll get hot.”
What does Freeman’s uptick mean for the Dodgers?
With the best rotation in baseball, the Dodgers are left scrounging around for offense any way that they can find it.
Teoscar Hernandez, Josue De Paula, and Mookie Betts have been the most consistent sources, with Max Muncy and Will Smith in the picture as well.
Still, the Dodgers need as many players in a spot as possible to deliver timely hits, and Freeman’s experience and skills make him a clear-cut candidate to step up.
To deliver results quickly, as he manages his knee and struggles, Freeman has made a mechanical change, getting out in front of the ball to catch it earlier on his bat.
The result may be less clean contact and hard hits, but more consistent contact, with the idea that it makes him valuable come the postseason.
“I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable,” he said. “I’m trying to find something that works for four weeks.”
Freeman has the right approach to deliver just what the Dodgers need. The entire offense does not need to be excellent; simply being good enough will lead to a three-peat.

CINCINNATI — Yoshinobu Yamamoto allowed one hit through seven innings as the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Cincinnati Reds 4-0 on Tuesday night to edge closer to an NL West division title.
The Dodgers reduced the magic number to clinch their 13th division title in the past 14 seasons to two. Los Angeles wrapped up a playoff spot on Monday and still is vying for the top seed in the NL.
Cincinnati is assured of a non-winning season after its 81st loss.
Yamamoto (14-8) made his team-high 27th start and allowed only a third-inning double to Elly De La Cruz, after which he retired 10 straight. He walked two and struck out seven. It was the second straight game a Dodgers starter went seven scoreless after Tarik Skubal on Monday.
Dodgers pitching recorded its 12th shutout of the season. The Reds were blanked for the 17th time.
Freddie Freeman returned to the Dodgers lineup after missing three of the past five games with right knee soreness and had three singles in five at-bats. Freeman was 3 for 30 coming into Tuesday.
Josue De Paula batted leadoff for the first time in just his fifth career game for the Dodgers and went 0 for 5 with a strikeout. He's 2 for 14 since his callup.
Teoscar Hernandez's 15th homer of the season off right-hander Rhett Lowder followed a walk to Kyle Tucker and made the score 3-0 in the third. Lowder (6-11) allowed three earned runs on five hits in five innings.
Alex Freeland made the score 4-0 in the seventh with a solo homer off Pierce Johnson.
De La Cruz extended his on-base streak to 22 games dating to Aug. 22, going 2 for 3 with a double, walk, and stolen base.
Cincinnati had runners on first and third in the ninth against Tanner Scott who struck out the next three batters to seal the Dodgers' ninth straight win over the Reds.
Dodgers LHP Blake Snell (4-1, 1.91) will oppose Reds LHP Andrew Abbott (6-11, 4.84) on Wednesday.

How Teoscar Hernández fixed his swing to help power Dodgers over the Reds
- Click here to listen to this article
-
CINCINNATI — A simple change opened a dramatic offensive turnaround for Dodgers left fielder Teoscar Hernández.
Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday, in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win against the Reds, was his second home run in as many nights, as the team trimmed its magic number to clinch the division to one behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s seven innings of one-hit ball. And, significantly, this one was against a right-handed pitcher.
“It’s been very helpful,” manager Dave Roberts said after the game. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. And the last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him.”
Through the end of August, Hernández had just a .668 OPS against right-handed pitchers this season. So, when Roberts was asked in Detroit whether the Dodgers would consider setting up a left-field platoon with the team’s September call-ups, he said yes.
Hernández homered off Tigers left-hander Framber Valdez on the last day of the series. And before the Dodgers opened a three-game set against the Cardinals at Dodger Stadium, Hernández met with the hitting coaches.
Against Valdez, Hernández was in a closed stance, to delay his front hip from opening, according to Dodgers hitting coach Aaron Bates. But the team’s hitting group thought a return to a familiar setup could be a long-term solution.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
In the past, Hernández had used a “twister tap” as his stride. He started in a more open stance, tapped his toe in line with the pitcher, and then set his foot down. But lower-body injuries the last couple of years — a left groin strain last season and a left hamstring strain earlier this season — forced him away from it.
His improved health and hip flexibility opened the avenue for him to return to that timing mechanism.
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
The advantage of the twister tap, as Hernández explained it, is how repeatable it is. A more traditional stride can be sped up or slowed down.
“Just being able to control my body and being in a good position,” Hernández said earlier this month. “I can see the pitch a little sooner and identify what kind of pitch it is and if it’s going to be a strike or a ball.”
With that change, he’s rewarded the Dodgers for deciding against platooning left field. Hernández entered Tuesday with a .777 OPS against right-handed pitchers — a sample size of just 28 plate appearances but still a significant jump.
“The biggest thing is his plate coverage away,” Bates said. “Because now he can spoil pitches, and he’s staying in at-bats longer.”
Hernández’s dramatic offensive turnaround, along with fellow corner outfielder Kyle Tucker’s improvement, have helped steady a Dodgers offense that’s missing Shohei Ohtani (on the IL with right biceps and left knee injuries) and includes a hobbled Freddie Freeman (right knee soreness).
Rookie Josue De Paula, mostly filling in for Ohtani at designated hitter, has already shown he can take mature at-bats and provide some pop. But he’s still finding his footing in a new league.
It lengthens the Dodgers lineup for Hernández, after a slow start to his year, to return to being a veteran power threat — just in time to, ideally, carry the momentum into the postseason.
On Monday, he launched his two-run shot off left-hander Nick Lodolo. On Tuesday, he replicated the feat off right-hander Rhett Lowder.
On the second pitch of the at-bat, Hernández recognized a hung slider, and he roped it over the left-field fence at 109.3 mph, according to Statcast. The blast put the Dodgers up 3-0 in the third inning, with Dodgers starter Yamamoto settling into a groove on the other side.
Yamamoto had walked the first two batters he faced, but he reined in his control to pitch seven scoreless innings and allow just one more baserunner — a double by Reds star shortstop Elly De La Cruz.
The Dodgers also scored on Hunter Feduccia’s second-inning single and Alex Freeland’s seventh-inning homer. And the Dodgers bullpen completed the shutout.
Freeman staying in the lineup
Freeman was all smiles after his three-hit game Tuesday — after going hitless for his last four games.
“I was supposed to be off tomorrow, but I played myself in there,” he said. “So I’m very excited.”
Roberts explained: “He was joking, saying, ‘If I get three hits, then can I be in there tomorrow?’”
Sure enough, the mechanical adjustments he made in the batting cage — focusing on getting his foot down early and making contact out in front — got him there.
“I’m just trying to find something that gives me results,” Freeman said. “We’re at the time where we’re just trying to get hot for five weeks here. So kind of like I did in the World Series a couple years ago, I did the step-out move. That’s not sustainable over six months. I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable.”
Though Roberts has been trying to find opportunities to rest Freeman, he saw promising signs Tuesday beyond the results.
“Just my eyes, just watching him move, I feel good about him going tomorrow,” Roberts said.
De Paula, Freeland and third baseman Max Muncy will be out of the lineup Wednesday, Roberts said.
